Toutes les trois issues de la génération: All three members of Generation 1.5, Rimel Mehleb, Sabrina Zennia and Bouchera Belhadj are the creators of the podcast Génération 1.5. Photo: Marine Caleb
« Les enfants qui ont migré sans en avoi: “Children who migrated without having chosen to”: that is how Rimel Mehleb, Sabrina Zennia and Bouchera Belhadj define Generation 1.5, their generation. It is an invisible, silent population, and the three women, who arrived from Algeria as children or teenagers, wanted to give it a voice by creating<l1> a podcast of the same name,</l1> launched on July 12. Their project sheds light on the lives and challenges of these uprooted young people left to fend for themselves.
À l’occasion de la Journée international: On International Youth Day, it seems crucial to talk about this generation of immigrants that has fallen through the cracks.
« J’ai migré avec mes parents quand j’av: “I migrated with my parents when I was 14. It was in March 2002,” says Andres Larrea. His father decided very quickly that he wanted to leave. “I didn’t have much time to prepare,” says Andres, conveying the shock and the rupture he was about to go through. His family and he went through the United States before crossing the border on foot and claiming asylum in Canada. After a stay at the YMCA, they settled in Montréal-Nord and obtained permanent residence three years later.
Andres était la seule personne de sa fam: Andres was the only person in his family who spoke English, so he had to help his parents with all the administrative procedures. He says this changed the dynamic in his family: “I had to take on responsibilities and become an active member of the family. It was a lot of stress.” It fell to him to inform his family about the Quebec system and, above all, to be a direct witness to his parents’ struggles.
Andres is part of Generation 1.5. The term was introduced by Cuban-American sociologist Rubén G. Rumbaut in the 1960s. Usually, people speak of first, second and even third generations of immigration to refer, respectively, to immigrants who migrated themselves, and to the children and grandchildren of those immigrants.
La génération 1.5, ce sont les enfants e: Generation 1.5 is made up of children and teenagers who were born abroad and left their country with their families to settle elsewhere. They have therefore lived in both their country of origin and their host country, and often hold both nationalities. Uprooted, they are in fact caught between two cultures: Quebecers without quite being Quebecers, and Peruvian, Algerian or Senegalese without fully sharing the same codes.
Comme tant d’autres, la famille d’Andres: Like so many others, Andres’s family migrated to give their children a better future, a quality education, the freedom to be who they are, and security. Because he spoke English, Andres bore the full brunt of his family’s difficulties. “You see the sacrifice and the loss of status, it’s very concrete. You know what they lost,” says Sabrina Zennia, at a meeting with the other creators of the podcast at Café Colibri on Beaubien Street, a multicultural café that has become a gathering place for many communities.
C’est sans oublier la pression à réussir: And that’s without mentioning the pressure to make something of your life, as if the children carried the weight of success. Faced with these expectations, the 1.5 child has to carve out a place in the host society, sometimes in contradiction with the culture of origin. “It’s as if the family was telling us, ‘Be better than the Quebecers, but stay like us,’” sighs Rimel. Every family has its own dynamic: some decide to maintain a strong connection to the country of origin, its values and its practices, while others prefer to set it aside in order to assimilate.
Pour les 1.5, les difficultés ne s’arrêt: For the 1.5s, the difficulties don’t stop at the family and these dualities. They begin with the departure and the arrival. For adults who choose to migrate as much as for children who have no say, leaving remains a rupture filled with doubt, fear and incomprehension. It is a total loss of bearings, and everything has to be relearned: how to say hello, how to dress, everyday gestures, the snack packed for 10 a.m., the language you have to learn to speak, read and write, the names that are so familiar and comforting to some but distressing to others, and so on. “It’s like we had to climb a mountain every time,” says Alilou, who arrived from Algeria at age 12, in the podcast’s second episode.
« Parmi les défis, il y a d’abord l’inté: “Among the challenges, there’s first school integration, francization, which is a big piece, but also building a social circle,” lists Marina Doucerain, a professor of social and cultural psychology who herself belongs to Generation 1.5. “I spent almost a year out of school and I didn’t know anyone,” says Andres, who felt very isolated when he arrived. “And with the stress my family was going through, I didn’t feel comfortable going through a teenage crisis,” he explains.
Et puis, il y a les discriminations ou t: And then there is discrimination, or simply the fact of being constantly singled out and asked where you’re from. “I arrived at the time of the first reasonable accommodation debates. I’ve always lived in a Quebec where immigration is portrayed as a threat,” says the young man.
Rimel Mehleb, Sabrina Zennia et Bouchera: Rimel Mehleb, Sabrina Zennia and Bouchera Belhadj regret that children’s feelings are not taken into account. Because the migration was undertaken for the children’s future and well-being, it is common to assume that they are lucky to be in Canada and that they will adapt quickly. The term Generation 1.5 is, moreover, little known, and this population remains understudied, or at least little visible.
Un constat que la psychologue Marina Dou: Psychologist Marina Doucerain shares this observation, although she cannot say what causes it. In any case, no one talks about it, not even those most directly affected. “Nobody talks about this, and it’s not just a coincidence. There is a lot of shame, guilt, secrecy, a lack of space around the subject,” says Rimel Mehleb.
C’est d’ailleurs la raison pour laquelle: That is precisely why Bouchera, Rimel and Sabrina created their podcast: “At first, we started it for ourselves. We wanted to document and open up the conversation on the subject, and to have it resonate with people.” Little by little, this intimate project has grown, loosening tongues and creating connections among these many experiences of migration.
La génération 1.5 se sent délaissée, liv: Generation 1.5 feels abandoned, left to fend for itself to understand its new environment and to mourn the one it left behind. Faced with a lack of support, with no help, reference points or role models, young people of Generation 1.5 make do. Some maintain a strong connection to their culture of origin through food, music, trips back to the home country, politics, religion or community. That is the case for Rimel, who retreated into her Algerian community after the debate over the Charter of Values and the hardening of the debate on secularism and immigration.
Pour Andres, après avoir voulu être « pl: For Andres, after wanting to be “whiter than white,” he now makes a point of maintaining a “cultural and, above all, culinary continuity.” “Language is very important to me. I can’t imagine not teaching it to my children, for example, it would be terrible,” the young man continues. Today an environmental science researcher and deeply politically engaged, Andres lives between Quebec and South America. “It helps me not feel like a stranger in my own country and catch up on all the slang!” he laughs.
Du point de vue de la psychologue Marina: From the point of view of psychologist Marina Doucerain, this making do could reflect “society’s failure.” “There’s some good in it, because they need to build connections. But it’s a problem if those connections are made out of spite, because there’s nothing else for them,” she says.
Lors de notre rencontre au café Colibri,: At our meeting at Café Colibri, Rimel, Bouchera and Sabrina denounce this neglect. “There are a lot of small initiatives, but they’re scattered and uncoordinated. There is no government plan,” laments Sabrina Zennia.
Stephan Reichhold, directeur de la Table: Stephan Reichhold, director of the Table de concertation des organismes au service des personnes réfugiées et immigrantes (TCRI), agrees: “Before, services for young people were only intended for refugees and immigrant youth aged 12 and under. The Ministry of Immigration didn’t feel concerned and said it should fall under the Ministry of Education.” Early childhood services existed, but 12- to 18-year-olds slipped under the radar.
Il explique qu’il y a eu un revirement d: He explains that there has been a turnaround over the past two years. In the wake of massive investments by the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) government, youth services have become a priority, according to Mr. Reichhold. “Many organizations have hired an intercultural community worker (ICI) for youth. There are collaborations with school boards,” he lists. “But we’re still not out of the woods, there is still a lot of effort needed, especially for those with precarious status, temporary workers, international students or asylum seekers,” Stephan Reichhold points out.
Contactés par courriel, le ministère de: Contacted by email, the Ministry of Immigration says it has hired 55 workers for youth, schools and early childhood in 20 community organizations across Quebec. “The ICIs promote the value of each young person, meeting others, conflict resolution, a sense of belonging and the discovery of activities in their communities,” says Arianne Méthot, the ministry’s communications manager. She adds that these workers offer intercultural support to “foster dialogue and reduce misunderstandings.”
Des efforts à instaurer dès la classe d’: Efforts that should begin in the welcome class, which Andres attended. “You realize it’s the government’s lowest priority when you look at the resources,” he laments. The young man believes teachers should get more support. “Teachers have to teach French, but also how Quebec society works. That’s a lot!” he says.
De son côté, Marina Doucerain estime que: For her part, Marina Doucerain believes young people, particularly preteens and teenagers, should be supported in building their “in-between” identity. “There should be an intervention or a program to help them create their narrative identity,” she explains. Narrative identity is the story each person tells about themselves, the narration that makes sense of things. “For parents, it’s simpler, because they are actors in the migration, they chose it. But for teens, for whom it’s already complicated, it’s a whole field of ruins to rebuild!” the psychologist elaborates.
Des idées qui répondraient aux témoignag: These are ideas that would respond to the testimonies of Generation 1.5 children collected by Bouchera, Rimel and Sabrina. They say they felt like a labour force, like their parents, workers who would benefit the Quebec economy. “The human side of migration is muted. And even when there are initiatives, they don’t get to the heart of the matter,” they assert. By opening up the conversation about their generation, they bring identity and culture back to the centre of the debate and remind us that “integration is vital and not just a whim.”
